paras: The Keysville white cap notices were written threats posted in June 1903 near Keysville, in Charlotte County, Virginia, ordering an unnamed Black woman to leave within ten days or be "roughly handled." The authors, who called themselves white caps and claimed fifteen members, were not identified, and the only known report is a short item in the Richmond Times-Dispatch.

The notices were posted in two places on outbuildings sometime before Saturday, June 13, 1903. Each warned "a colored woman" to leave in ten days, and the notice stated that fifteen men were "interested in the matter" and meant to carry out their threats. No reason for the order and no name for the woman appear in the report.

On June 13, Captain Thomas A. Spencer of the State Bank in Richmond passed through Keysville on his way to his farm about six miles away, where he planned to visit his uncle and aunt and to investigate the notices. The wording suggests the outbuildings stood on or near that farm, though the report does not say so directly. As of June 15 the suspected parties were not known, and no later report of arrests, of harm to the woman, or of her leaving was found.

The Richmond Times-Dispatch carried the story on June 16 in a column of Keysville correspondence dated June 15, under the headings "After White Caps" and "Captain Spencer Investigates Some Threatening Notices in Charlotte." The paragraph sat between an item about a traveling salesman who dislocated his shoulder and a notice of a local death, and it offered no comment on the threat. Its attention went to Spencer, a Richmond banker, rather than to the woman, who is identified only by race and sex.
No coverage of the notices was found in other white papers or in the Black press.
